title: Video streaming
brief: You run a movie and series service for a growing audience. Each viewer pulls a few seconds of video at a time for two hours straight. Bandwidth is the largest cost by far, and everyone wants to start watching in the evening.

clarify.q: Is most of the library watched equally?
clarify.a: No. A few hundred titles get most of the viewing. The long tail is watched rarely.

clarify.q: How long can a viewer wait for the picture to start?
clarify.a: About a second for each chunk. More than that and the picture freezes.

clarify.q: Do viewers need to be signed in?
clarify.a: Yes. A subscription check happens once at the start, not for every chunk.

clarify.q: What if a new season launches?
clarify.a: A huge crowd presses play on the same episode in the same hour. It is the busiest night of the quarter.

notes: Each viewer fetches one 2 MB chunk every 4 seconds.
Bandwidth is priced per gigabyte sent to viewers (about 4 cents at list price, approx.).

numbers.label: Video chunks per second at peak
Video sent to viewers in a month
numbers.how: about 0.5 GB/s average x 2.6 million seconds (approx.)

hints: A few titles get most of the views. How can you use that to protect your storage and your bill?
A CDN with an origin shield means one trip from storage serves thousands of viewers. Keep the library in object storage and move old titles to a colder tier.
A complete playable rendition is a publication invariant. A bounded lower-quality fallback preserves playback. Measure the failed boundary, waiting time and retry work before choosing a change.

editorial.summary: Video is a bandwidth problem. Put the video chunks on a CDN, add an origin shield so storage sees one request per chunk instead of thousands, and keep the long tail in cheaper storage. The account and catalog side is small and boring on purpose.

designs.name: CDN with origin shield
designs.why: Popular titles live on the CDN and almost never reach storage. The shield merges misses from every edge so the origin sees one request per chunk. App servers only handle login, browsing and play events.

tradeoffs: Every extra copy layer (edge, shield, storage) lowers your storage load, but each one adds a little delay for a rare title nobody has watched yet.
Serving fewer quality levels shrinks the bill but makes the picture worse on a fast connection.
A cold tier for rarely watched titles cuts storage cost. The first viewer of a rare title waits a few seconds longer.
Bandwidth cost dominates. Doubling the app servers barely changes the bill. Doubling the viewers doubles it.
editorial.realWorld: Large video services place their own cache boxes inside internet providers, so most of the traffic never crosses the public internet. Video can be well over a third of all downstream internet traffic in the evening (approx.).

correctness.prompt: Video streaming: which invariant does this trace protect, and what failure would break it?
correctness.discussion: Deliver versioned video segments while bounding cold-origin load and startup delay. Versioned segments prevent caches mixing different encodes. The heavy bottleneck is bytes and origin fanout, not metadata requests. A complete playable rendition is a publication invariant. A bounded lower-quality fallback preserves playback.

fields.label: Step 1. A viewer starts episode E. Which identity should its segments use?
options: An immutable manifest generation and quality-specific segment ids
fields.explanation: Versioned segments prevent caches mixing different encodes.

fields.label: Step 2. The new season misses at many edges at once. What happens at origin?
options: Collapse fills and cap fetch concurrency; measure startup buffering
fields.explanation: The heavy bottleneck is bytes and origin fanout, not metadata requests.

fields.label: Step 3. One quality encode is missing a segment. Publish its manifest?
options: Wait for validation or serve a validated lower quality
Advertise it and retry the missing segment indefinitely
fields.explanation: A complete playable rendition is a publication invariant. A bounded lower-quality fallback preserves playback.

correctness.responsibility: Deliver versioned video segments while bounding cold-origin load and startup delay.
correctness.limits: The traffic model does not execute this protocol. The checked trace covers its central responsibility; the written explanation is retained for review.

twist.brief: Demand has settled at about 150 requests/s. The new monthly ceiling is $43293. The original burst reserve now competes with the operating budget. Decide which reserve to keep, then test its failure headroom. All data and recovery promises still apply.

design.name: Smaller workload, measured reserve
design.why: Reduce the paid floor for the quieter workload, preserving the required copies and recovery settings. This design was checked through the full event day.
